desc:
Form every pair that takes one element from a and one from b; there are a.length * b.length such pairs. The distance of a pair is |x - y|. Pairs are counted separately even if they have equal distance.

Sort all pair distances in non-decreasing order and return the k-th one (1-indexed). The arrays are not sorted.

Example: for a = [1, 5], b = [2, 9] the distances are 1, 8, 3, 4, sorted 1, 3, 4, 8, so k = 3 gives 4.
hints: With up to 16 million pairs, building and sorting all distances is wasteful. Search over the distance value instead.
Sort b. For one element x of a and a limit d, the elements y with |x - y| ≤ d form a contiguous block of the sorted b: those in [x - d, x + d].
Count that block with two binary searches (bisect_right(b, x + d) - bisect_left(b, x - d)), sum over a, and binary search the smallest d whose total is at least k.
editorial: Let count(d) be the number of cross pairs with distance at most d. It is non-decreasing in d, and the smallest d with count(d) ≥ k is the k-th smallest distance (it is a real distance because the count only grows at values that occur).

Sort b once. For each x in a, the partners within distance d are exactly the values of b in [x - d, x + d], a contiguous range of the sorted array found with two binary searches. Summing gives count(d) in O(|a| log |b|).

The distance range is [0, max difference], which is at most 2·109 and fits in a signed 32-bit integer; about 31 iterations are needed. Total time O((|a| + |b|) log |b| + |a| log |b| log R). Searching on the answer is the key idea; a heap over all pairs would cost O(k log) and is far slower for large k.
